strengths: Careful physics-aware integration of 3DGS with cryo-EM image formation principles including CTF and Fourier slice theorem
Practical computational efficiency advantages (2-3× FPS improvement over cryoDRGN) with lower memory requirements
Comprehensive evaluation on four real cryo-EM datasets with standard quantitative metrics
Self-contained reconstruction capability from random initialization without requiring external consensus maps
Well-formulated mathematical framework connecting 3D Gaussian representations to observed cryo-EM projections
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily applies existing 3DGS technique to a new domain with engineering-level modifications rather than fundamental methodological innovation
Narrow, specialized scope with limited relevance to broad AI/ML community; better suited for domain-specific (structural biology/microscopy) venues

Incomplete and problematic baseline comparisons: unfair comparison with cryoDRGN (addresses heterogeneous vs. homogeneous reconstruction), missing comparisons with other classical cryo-EM methods and recent GMM approaches
Inconsistent and modest improvements: method underperforms on EMPIAR-10028 (3.80 Å vs. 2.49 Å for cryoDRGN); typical FSC improvements are 0.3-0.5 Å with no statistical significance testing
Questionable 'ab initio' claims: initialization uses image-based priors, not truly random; definition lacks precision compared to established ab initio reconstruction definitions
Lack of ground truth validation: evaluation uses only real experimental data without access to true 3D structures, making objective comparison impossible
Missing reproducibility details: no code availability, incomplete optimization specifications, CUDA implementation details insufficient for reproduction
Insufficient failure analysis and ablations: no discussion of failure modes, hyperparameter sensitivity, or principled Gaussian count selection
Limited theoretical justification: no analysis of why anisotropic Gaussians outperform isotropic ones; no convergence guarantees or principled framework

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: GMM-based methods for cryo-EM reconstruction despite their advantages over neural approaches
Principled technical approach with physics-informed formulation connecting 3D Gaussians to 2D cryo-EM images through Fourier slice theorem and CTF modulation
Comprehensive experimental validation on 4 real cryo-EM datasets with consistent improvements in FSC curves (e.g., 2.49 Å vs 4.07 Å on EMPIAR-10049 vs CryoDRGN)
Practical efficiency demonstrated: 2-3× faster convergence (5 vs 50+ epochs), low memory footprint (~380 MiB), and CUDA-accelerated implementation
Thorough ablation studies investigating impact of Gaussian count and comprehensive implementation details enabling reproducibility
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations and well-organized writing making the work accessible to both AI and structural biology audiences
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily adapts existing 3DGS technique (Kerbl et al. 2023) to cryo-EM rather than proposing fundamentally new methods; Fourier-slice-based projection uses well-established cryo-EM theory

Initialization dependency contradicts 'self-contained' claim: Appendix A reveals non-trivial initialization strategy with spherical region constraints and statistical grounding; unclear sensitivity to initialization choices

Narrow applicability scope restricted to homogeneous reconstruction: assumes all particles correspond to single identical structure; majority of real cryo-EM data exhibits heterogeneity (multiple conformational states) with no proposed pathway for extension

Incomplete baseline comparisons: no experimental comparison with recent methods (CryoSTAR, DynaMight, Chen 2025) despite citations; limited breakdown of why CryoSplat outperforms CryoDRGN (method vs implementation); missing comparisons with traditional RELION-style methods

Evaluation limitations: FSC metric alone doesn't validate biological correctness; no comparison against known atomic structures; only 4 datasets tested; lacks statistical analysis and confidence intervals

Unaddressed scalability questions: how does method perform at sub-Ångström resolutions, on membrane proteins, or with rare symmetries; Figure 3 shows performance plateau after 10,000 Gaussians raising questions about sufficiency

Oversimplified loss function: MSE loss (Eq. 14) may not capture structural priors important for cryo-EM; positioning simplicity as advantage potentially understates limitations; no exploration of alternative formulations
Runtime context insufficient: Figure 4 lacks absolute reference; total GPU time for complete reconstruction not specified; scalability to larger datasets not demonstrated
Missing failure mode analysis: no discussion of challenging cases, structural properties leading to poor reconstruction, or robustness to pose errors and noise

Interpretability gap: while GMMs claimed more interpretable than neural networks, 30,000 Gaussians still lack clear biological meaning; individual Gaussian correspondence to molecular structure components not analyzed

strengths: Clear motivation addressing specific cryo-EM challenges with well-reasoned physics-based design choices (orthogonal projection, normalization term for quantitative correctness)

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple datasets with extensive ablations (Gaussian count, initialization strategies, isotropic vs. anisotropic), strong quantitative results (3.3-4.26 Å resolution)
Excellent reproducibility support with full mathematical derivations, algorithmic pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, and robustness demonstrations across initialization strategies
Strong empirical performance showing competitive or superior FSC curves compared to established baselines (cryoSPARC, cryoDRGN) on four diverse EMPIAR datasets with varying complexity
Thoughtful domain-specific adaptations of 3DGS framework including tile-based rasterization for cryo-EM memory efficiency and FFT-aligned coordinates
weaknesses: Severely limited novelty: core contribution is straightforward adaptation of existing 3DGS (Kerbl et al. 2023) with incremental engineering modifications (orthogonal projection, normalization term, FFT alignment) rather than fundamental methodological innovation

No convincing justification for GMM representation choice over neural field methods: missing systematic comparison with cryoDRGN and other neural approaches; no quantitative evidence that GMMs are fundamentally superior to neural networks for this task

Critical scope limitation: method restricted to homogeneous reconstruction (all particles from single structure), which is acknowledged only briefly; unable to handle compositional or conformational heterogeneity prevalent in real cryo-EM datasets, severely limiting practical applicability

Overstated physical accuracy claims: orthogonal projection is itself an approximation; real cryo-EM involves CTF modulation, contrast transfer, beam damage not modeled here; framing as 'physically accurate' is misleading

Insufficient validation and analysis: FSC metric can be gamed by spurious high-frequency features; limited comparison with heterogeneous reconstruction methods; no failure case analysis; only 10 random seeds for initialization robustness claim; normalization term importance shown to be minimal by corrected FSC analysis in D.4

Simple optimization formulation lacking sophistication: plain MSE loss without noise-aware weighting, outlier handling, or robust statistics; no regularization despite extremely noisy input data; insufficient for real cryo-EM variations
Unclear practical advantages: paper does not establish when practitioners should choose CryoSplat over cryoSPARC or cryoDRGN; no analysis of use cases or decision criteria

Incomplete technical justification: Gaussian parameterization choice not justified; alternative projection approximations not compared; individual physical modeling components not ablated; scaling to large complexes not discussed
Reproducibility concerns despite good documentation: actual code release not provided (only promised as future work); for specialized methods, source code crucial for adoption and validation

strengths: Novel and physically-motivated adaptation of Gaussian splatting to cryo-EM with careful implementation of orthogonal projection, CTF modulation, and FFT-aligned coordinates
Self-contained pipeline achieving stable reconstruction from random initialization without external consensus maps, demonstrated through convincing initialization ablations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four diverse real cryo-EM datasets with thorough quantitative (FSC) and qualitative comparisons
Consistent superior performance across datasets, particularly on challenging structures with heterogeneity or conformational flexibility
Efficient CUDA implementation with detailed runtime/memory analysis showing practical utility (up to 30x faster than baselines)
Extensive ablation studies examining number of Gaussians, anisotropy, SNR robustness, and initialization strategy
Clear presentation with informative figures and detailed reproducibility information including promised code release
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation obscured in claims: method requires known particle poses (from external consensus maps), not truly reconstruction 'without prior models' - significantly restricts applicability to post-processing rather than ab initio reconstruction
Limited to homogeneous reconstruction of single structural state; cannot handle heterogeneous variability common in real cryo-EM projects

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only three methods tested, missing recent neural NeRF approaches and state-of-the-art heterogeneous reconstruction methods; cryoDRGN settings potentially not controlled identically
FSC evaluation on same dataset (split halves) is optimistic; corrected FSC analysis (Appendix D.4) suggests potential resolution overestimation particularly at high Gaussian counts
Scalability concerns: memory increases substantially with Gaussian count; authors note 524K Gaussian regime 'impractical'; unclear for true atomic resolution or very large complexes
Limited guidance for hyperparameter selection (number of Gaussians N, decay parameter γ) on new datasets despite apparent dataset-dependent sensitivity shown in Figure 3
Theoretical justification lacking for key design choices: why simple MSE loss over probabilistic formulation, why Gaussian densification strategy optimal, no convergence analysis
Critical ablation missing: sensitivity to errors in input particle poses - essential for practical utility since known poses from external sources may contain systematic errors
Limited methodological novelty: primary contribution is engineering-focused application of existing Gaussian splatting with relatively straightforward physics adaptations
